Hi Claire — thanks again for taking the demo on Thursday. Quick follow-up to capture the SLO-related items you and Ben called out (so our eng team can scope the perf qualification runs). See below and a proposed checklist attached.

Key asks I captured during the call:
- Target latency SLOs: 95th percentile end-to-end <= 800ms for the patient-summary flow (typical payload: 300 tokens in, ~1,000 tokens out).
- Concurrency and throughput: baseline expected steady-state of 150 concurrent requests with spikes up to 400 concurrent during business hours.
- Streaming: UI requires first partial tokens within 150–250ms of request start for perceived responsiveness; full response can stream to completion.
- Context window: clinical context bundle ~12–16k tokens (history + patient record). Most requests will include a 14k token context with variable output up to 2k tokens.
- Fallback behavior: must gracefully degrade if we can't meet the SLO (e.g., limit output tokens, switch to a lower-capacity model, or return progressive summary + ask user to request full report).

Initial implications and risks (engineering perspective):
- 14k context + 2k output increases decoding time significantly; without streaming, 95th percentiles are likely to exceed 800ms on our current GPU profiles.
- Continuous batching helps throughput but adds headroom latency; at your concurrency target (150–400) we need to tune batching windows aggressively to keep tail latency predictable.
- Streaming is the biggest lever for perceived latency — we can meet the 150–250ms first-token target with progressive KV cache priming and low-latency I/O if we pin instances to smaller batch depths.

Proposed next steps (I added these to the attached checklist):
1) Schedule a short perf-qual run with Polaris sample traces (you to share). We recommend two passes:
   - Pass A: median latency profile at expected payload (14k in / 1k out) focusing on throughput baseline at 150 concurrent.
   - Pass B: tail latency with spikes (simulate 400 concurrent for 10 minute bursts) and evaluate streaming-first-token times.
2) Karthik/Markus will prepare two config variants to test:
   - Config 1: prioritized latency (lower batching, auto-stream) using 8-bit quantized model variant.
   - Config 2: prioritized throughput (larger batches, caching) with fallback to a cheaper model variant for non-critical requests.
3) Gather the sample PII-scrubbed traces and share by Tue morning so we can run a quick bench on Wed.

Can you confirm the first-token target (150–250ms) and whether you have any hard limits on output truncation? Once you confirm, Karthik will pick configs and we’ll lock the perf window.

Thanks — attaching the SLO checklist and the perf-bench template.

Priya / Markus — quick internal note before we run benches. My assumptions and suggested config knobs:
- Model variant: start with the 16k-capacity Llama-XL quantized to int8 (known perf on our M100 nodes). Keep a 4-bit variant as a fallback.
- Batching: target < 6ms additional queuing for latency config (Config 1). That means batch cutoffs ~4–6 concurrent requests per GPU depending on arrival patterns.
- Streaming: enable progressive decode with a 40-token microflush cadence to push first tokens out early; the network stack must prioritize the first-chunk frames.
- KV cache warmup: pre-load common patient-slot embeddings where possible; this saves ~30–60ms per request in our internal runs.
- Measurement: measure both first-token time and decode tail; record p50/p90/p95/p99 and percent of requests that meet the 200ms first-token target.

I’ll prep two Docker configs today and we can run the first pass on Wed morning. Markus — can you sanity-check the M100 capacity estimate and whether we should reserve dedicated instances for Polaris during the bench window?
